question: A 10-month-old infant in Delhi presents in January with acute watery, non-bloody diarrhoea and moderate dehydration. Stool shows no leucocytes. Which structural feature of the most likely causative virus is characteristic on electron microscopy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rotavirus — the single most important cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in Indian children under 5 — has a characteristic triple-layered capsid appearing 'wheel-like' on EM (Latin: rota = wheel). Winter peak, 6 months–2 years age group, and non-enveloped dsRNA with 11 segments are key features.

answers.text: Enveloped helical nucleocapsid with single negative-sense RNA strand

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes paramyxovirus morphology (e.g. measles, RSV). Rotavirus is non-enveloped with segmented dsRNA — a critical difference affecting environmental survival.

answers.text: Small non-enveloped icosahedral capsid with cup-shaped depressions on the surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes caliciviruses (Norovirus), which cause outbreaks in closed communities. While important in older children and adults, Rotavirus remains the leading cause of severe infant diarrhoea in India.
This describes rhabdoviruses (Rabies virus). Rotavirus has icosahedral symmetry with a distinctive triple-layered capsid, not bullet morphology.

overallFeedback.feedback: Rotavirus: non-enveloped, dsRNA, 11 segments, triple-layered icosahedral capsid = 'wheel-like' on EM. Most important cause of severe infant diarrhoea in India; winter peak; diagnosis by stool antigen ELISA.
The 'wheel-like' triple-layered capsid on EM is Rotavirus's signature. It is non-enveloped (survives on fomites) with 11 dsRNA segments.
